column5: break fallow ground; sow righteousness; harvest steadfast love
column6: Commentary makes fieldwork a figure for growth into lasting good; Hosea directly joins breaking uncultivated soil and sowing justice to a harvest of love, adding a moral yield to the image.

column5: cleansing joined to multiplied grain
column6: The commentary joins z-k-w's growth and purification senses; Ezekiel promises both rescue from uncleanness and multiplied grain, explicitly coupling moral cleansing with field abundance.

column5: God supplies seed and multiplies harvest of righteousness
column6: Commentary links crop growth, giving, and purification; Paul says God supplies seed, increases it, and multiplies the harvest of righteousness, making generosity productive in righteousness.

column5: sowing generously and reaping generously
column6: The commentary pictures a share given from growing produce; Paul makes generosity itself sowing whose return is measured at harvest, extending the crop image to giving.

column5: rain-fed land yields useful crop and receives blessing
column6: Commentary contrasts cultivated yield with failed wild growth; Hebrews says land drinking rain and producing useful crops for cultivators is blessed, making productive reception of rain the positive outcome.

column5: thorns yield curse and burning
column6: Against the commentary's cultivated crop that is harvested and its failing pasture, Hebrews' same rain-fed ground can instead bear thorns, be rejected, and end in burning; it sharpens the field's two outcomes.

column5: tithe brought to the storehouse; blessing poured out
column6: The commentary describes a measured share given from produce; Malachi requires the full tithe and promises overflowing blessing, joining a crop's due to its continued abundance.

column5: devourer restrained; vine keeps its fruit
column6: The commentary's due-paid crop leaves a clean remainder; after the tithe, Malachi says the destroyer will not ruin produce and the vine will not fail, explicitly protecting what remains.

column5: one plants, another waters, God gives growth
column6: The commentary's field needs cultivation and growth; Paul distinguishes planting and watering from God's giving the increase, locating the crop's growth in divine care.

column5: God's field and fellow workers
column6: The commentary reads Rabb through tending a farm; Paul calls the community God's field and its ministers God's coworkers, turning stewardship of a field into a communal image.

column5: first fruits from threshing floor, wine press, oxen, and sheep
column6: The commentary describes a share of produce being given; the Didache specifies first fruits from harvest and livestock for prophets, or for the poor if no prophet is present, making the due a concrete communal practice.

column5: alms extinguish sin like water extinguishes fire
column6: The commentary says the crop's given share purifies what remains; Sirach directly compares alms to water quenching fire and says it atones for sin, supplying a Jewish formulation of giving as purification.

column5: almsgiving purges sin
column6: The commentary connects the paid share with cleansing; Tobit says almsgiving delivers from death and purges sin, explicitly giving charity a purifying and saving effect.

column5: the field corner has no fixed minimum measure
column6: The commentary treats a known measured share as due from produce; Peah instead assigns a field's corner to the poor without a fixed minimum, showing a neighboring Jewish harvest due with a deliberately different measure.

column5: corners of the field and gleanings left for poor and sojourner
column6: The commentary's grown crop yields a portion owed; Leviticus leaves field edges and gleanings for the poor and resident alien, making the share a right taken directly from harvest.

column5: vineyard gleanings and fallen grapes left for poor and sojourner
column6: The commentary's due comes from a crop and purifies its remainder; Leviticus applies the same harvest rule to grapes, showing the share across a second cultivated product.

column5: a forgotten sheaf left for stranger, orphan, and widow
column6: The commentary's field produces a share that is given; Deuteronomy assigns even an accidentally forgotten sheaf to vulnerable neighbors, specifying a harvest right rather than mere generosity.

column5: tithe of seed and fruit belongs to YHWH
column6: The commentary's crop gives rise to a measured due; Leviticus marks the tithe of field seed and tree fruit as holy to YHWH, giving the agricultural share a sacred status.

column5: tithe of annual field increase
column6: The commentary's crop yields a fixed share; Deuteronomy requires a tithe of all yearly seed-field produce, making the recurring harvest the basis of the due.

column5: third-year tithe stored in towns
column6: The commentary describes measured yield paid out; Deuteronomy's third-year tithe is stored locally, setting aside produce for Levite and vulnerable neighbors.

column5: Levite, stranger, orphan, and widow eat and are satisfied
column6: The commentary says the share given purifies what remains; this verse states who receives the stored tithe and that they eat their fill, adding the social result of the crop's due.

column5: first fruits presented before YHWH
column6: The commentary's cultivated product has a right paid from it; Deuteronomy makes the first of the land's produce a presentation to YHWH, a distinct first-fruit form of the due.

column5: one fifth of the harvest given to Pharaoh; four fifths kept for seed and food
column6: The commentary defines kharāj as a known annual amount removed from property; Joseph's statute assigns one fifth of Egypt's harvest to Pharaoh and leaves the rest to the cultivator, concretely pairing due and remainder.

column5: one fifth of produce established as a continuing land tax
column6: The commentary links the crop's annual yield to a measured due; Genesis says Joseph made the one-fifth payment a standing statute, an unusually close fiscal counterpart to the commentary's fixed annual amount.

column5: Levites give a tenth of the tithe they receive
column6: The commentary follows a share given from produce with what remains after payment; Numbers requires Levites to set aside a tenth of their own tithe, showing a due passed onward from a due.

column5: the Levites' offering counted as grain from threshing floor and wine from press
column6: The commentary's share comes from harvested produce; Numbers explicitly treats the Levites' contribution as threshing-floor grain and wine-press yield, joining obligation to agricultural output.

column5: Isaac sows, reaps a hundredfold, and is blessed
column6: The commentary joins seed growth to success; Isaac's literal sowing and hundredfold harvest in the same year are explicitly attributed to YHWH's blessing, giving the agricultural success a narrated instance.

column5: plowing and harrowing before sowing
column6: The commentary says falāḥ names splitting the soil and the farmer who does it; Isaiah asks whether the plowman keeps plowing and opening the ground all day, directly placing soil-breaking before the crop.

column5: different seeds scattered after leveling the field
column6: The commentary develops a worked field into growing produce; Isaiah describes leveling the surface and sowing distinct crops in their places, adding the ordered steps between plowing and yield.

column5: God waters furrows and softens ridges, blessing growth
column6: The commentary links divine blessing to seed growth; the psalm depicts God saturating and leveling furrows and blessing their growth, making cultivation and increase part of God's care.

column5: the year crowned with goodness and abundance
column6: The commentary joins success to remaining in good; the psalm says God crowns the year with goodness and abundance overflows, connecting agricultural yield with goodness across a whole year.

column5: pastures clothed and valleys covered with grain
column6: The commentary contrasts failing pasture with cultivated produce; the psalm pictures pasture and valley alike clothed with flocks and grain, adding a scene of abundant land rather than withering grass.

column5: bread shared with the hungry and the homeless sheltered
column6: The commentary says a share is given from one's product; Isaiah defines the fast through sharing bread and taking the poor into one's house, making the ethical claim on one's provision concrete.

column5: the generous person becomes a watered garden and unfailing spring
column6: The commentary joins giving with growth and lasting good; Isaiah promises that the one guided by YHWH will be like a watered garden whose waters do not fail, making generosity's result enduring and fertile.

column5: rain makes earth bud, supplying seed to sower and bread to eater
column6: The commentary says seed grows by God's blessing; Isaiah's rain and snow make the earth bud and provide both seed and bread, spelling out the movement from divine water to future sowing and present food.

column5: tree by water bears fruit, leaf does not wither, and prospers
column6: The commentary links growth to success that remains in good; the psalm's planted tree bears fruit in season and does not wither, joining productive growth to persistence.

column5: human placed in garden to work and keep it
column6: The commentary reads Rabb as undertaking the repair and care of a farm; Genesis gives the human the work of serving and guarding the garden, adding the cultivator's assigned stewardship.

column5: grass and flower fade, but God's word stands forever
column6: The commentary contrasts pasture that perishes with the field yield that remains in good; Isaiah explicitly sets fading vegetation against what lasts forever, sharpening the contrast of transience and permanence.

column5: righteous flourish like palm and cedar planted in God's courts
column6: The commentary joins success with growth that remains in good; the psalm makes the righteous flourish as long-lived planted trees, adding an image of rooted persistence.

column5: righteous still bear fruit in old age
column6: The commentary links growth to enduring good; the psalm's righteous remain fresh and fruitful in old age, making continuing yield a sign of lasting vitality.

column5: God makes grass for cattle and plants for human food
column6: The commentary contrasts pasture that fades with cultivated yield; the psalm says God makes grass for animals and plants humans cultivate for food, distinguishing provision for both pasture and field.

column5: uncultivated vine and spontaneous growth left unreaped in sabbath year
column6: The commentary says wild pasture dries and is carried away while a worked field bears owed produce; Leviticus forbids harvesting spontaneous sabbath growth, assigning the unworked year's yield a protected use rather than treating it as waste.

column5: uncultivated yield is food for domestic and wild animals
column6: The commentary contrasts fading pasture with fruitful cultivation; Leviticus makes the sabbath land's spontaneous growth food for animals, a different valuation of land left unworked.

column5: vineyard owner digs, clears stones, plants vines, and expects grapes
column6: The commentary describes a field being worked for its product; Isaiah's owner prepares a vineyard carefully but gets wild grapes, making failed yield a narrative counterpoint to the crop whose due is paid.

column5: vineyard stands for Israel; God sought justice and found bloodshed
column6: The commentary's field image connects produce with what is rightly owed; Isaiah interprets the vineyard's failed fruit as Israel's failure of justice, adding an ethical measure to agricultural yield.

column5: Israel's mountains will bear branches and fruit for the people
column6: The commentary's planted field grows and yields its product; Ezekiel promises the restored land will branch and bear fruit for Israel, making field fertility a sign of restoration.

column5: God restores the years eaten by locusts
column6: The commentary contrasts a pasture that dries and disappears with enduring yield; Joel promises the crop years consumed by locusts will be restored, offering a recovery from agricultural loss.

column5: one scatters freely and yet increases
column6: The commentary joins giving a portion to continued increase; Proverbs says one who scatters freely grows richer, directly pairing generosity with growth while leaving the mechanism proverbial.

column5: the generous person is enriched and the waterer watered
column6: The commentary joins crop growth to a share given; Proverbs says the one who refreshes others will be refreshed, extending the field's reciprocity into an ethical maxim.

column5: good soil hears and bears a crop at differing yields
column6: The commentary pictures a worked field whose crop grows and is harvested; Jesus interprets good soil as hearing and bearing fruit, with thirty-, sixty-, or hundredfold yield, making receptivity and productivity explicit.

column5: good soil holds the word and bears fruit with patience
column6: The commentary joins growth to lasting good; Luke's good soil holds the word in an honest heart and bears fruit with endurance, linking soil, inner purification, and persistence.

column5: seed grows while the farmer sleeps and rises
column6: The commentary says the crop grows through divine blessing; Mark's farmer does not know how the seed sprouts and grows, emphasizing growth not controlled by the cultivator.

column5: grain ripe, the sickle is put in because harvest has come
column6: The commentary's success becomes a lasting crop; Mark's parable ends with ripe grain and harvest, supplying the endpoint of the growth process.

column5: fruit-bearing branch is pruned so it bears more fruit
column6: The commentary joins purification with crop increase; Jesus uses καθαίρει, a verb for pruning or cleansing, of the already fruitful branch, explicitly meeting purification and increased fruit.

column5: vineyard owner prepares the vineyard and leases it to tenants
column6: The commentary reads Rabb as one who undertakes a property's repair and care; Jesus' owner plants, fences, equips, and leases a vineyard, a close scene of the cultivator's stewardship.

column5: owner sends servants to collect the vineyard's produce
column6: The commentary says the crop has a due portion; the vineyard owner sends servants at harvest to receive its fruit, making the owner's claim on cultivated yield explicit.

column5: sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life
column6: The commentary joins a cultivated yield with what is better and more enduring; Paul makes sowing to the Spirit yield eternal life, transferring the harvest to the afterlife.

column5: rains and fruitful seasons fill people with food and gladness
column6: The commentary attributes growth to divine blessing; Paul points to God giving rain and fruitful seasons, joining crop provision with nourishment and joy.

column5: generosity lays up a foundation for the future and real life
column6: The commentary links paying the crop's due with what lasts; Timothy's instruction joins generosity to a future foundation and taking hold of life, giving the share an explicitly lasting horizon.

column5: the seed sown in earth and its emergence as an image of resurrection
column6: The commentary contrasts perishing pasture with the crop that remains; Clement points to seed put in earth and its subsequent growth as evidence for resurrection, connecting agricultural persistence with life beyond death.

column5: no rain and no human to work the ground
column6: The commentary's field requires both growth and tending; Genesis says vegetation had not appeared because YHWH had not sent rain and there was no human to work the ground, giving a compact account of those conditions.

column5: desert becomes fruitful field when the spirit is poured out
column6: The commentary contrasts withered pasture with worked, productive land; Isaiah says wilderness becomes a fruitful field after the spirit is poured out, making transformed fertility a restoration image.

column5: celebration with Levite and sojourner over the land's good produce
column6: The commentary's harvest share is given to another; Deuteronomy commands rejoicing with Levite and stranger in the good YHWH gave, showing the produce's due ending in shared enjoyment.

column5: rain brings grain, wine, and oil
column6: The commentary attributes crop growth to blessing and God's care; Deuteronomy promises rain in its season and the resulting harvest, making rainfall the condition of the land's produce.

column5: olive tree beaten once; remainder left for stranger, orphan, and widow
column6: The commentary's share comes from a product while a remainder is kept; Deuteronomy limits harvesting olives to one pass so a remnant remains for vulnerable people, making restraint part of the due.

column5: vineyard gleaning left for stranger, orphan, and widow
column6: The commentary's crop yields a share for another; this verse applies the remnant rule to grapes, showing the harvest right in a third crop.

column5: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; speaker says he purified his heart in vain
column6: The commentary labels Arabic z-k-w for purification as well as growth; the psalmist uses Hebrew זכה for keeping his heart pure and pairs it with washing his hands, a cognate used for purity amid a crisis of reward.

column5: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; who can claim a clean heart?
column6: The commentary connects purification to paying a crop's due; Proverbs uses Hebrew זכה to ask who can claim to have made the heart pure from sin, focusing the cognate on moral cleanness.

column5: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; can a mortal be pure before God?
column6: The commentary uses z-k-w for purification; Job uses Hebrew זכה in asking whether a human can be pure, adding a skeptical limit on claims of self-cleansing.

column5: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; how can a human be justified and clean before God?
column6: The commentary links purification with the crop's paid share; Bildad uses Hebrew זכה in questioning human purity before God, a cognate that frames cleansing as a divine rather than merely accounting matter.

column5: break up fallow ground and do not sow among thorns
column6: The commentary's farmer splits and works the earth; Jeremiah uses plowing fallow ground as a call to change before sowing, making the fieldwork an ethical demand.

column5: sowing in tears and reaping in joy
column6: The commentary makes a crop's growth culminate in good that lasts; the psalm's mournful sowing gives way to joyful harvest, adding reversal from present labor to future reward.

column5: plowman overtakes reaper in a season of abundance
column6: The commentary's growth is a field's enduring success; Amos depicts grain harvest and grape harvest overlapping, intensifying the crop image into restored abundance.

column5: heavens shut, rain withheld, and land's produce lost
column6: The commentary contrasts a field that grows and yields its due with a pasture that fades; Deuteronomy describes the inverse, disobedience bringing no rain and a land that fails to produce.

column5: almsgiving and cleanness; rendering of the Greek is disputed
column6: The commentary says a paid share purifies what remains; Luke's difficult instruction is commonly read as giving alms from what is within and says all is clean, directly associating alms with cleanness while the exact wording is uncertain.

column5: weeds gathered for burning while wheat is stored at harvest
column6: The commentary distinguishes failing wild growth from a cultivated crop that is gathered; Jesus' parable separates weeds for burning from wheat for the barn, making the different harvest fates explicit.

column5: murderous tenants refuse the owner's share and lose the vineyard
column6: The commentary's successful field grows, pays its due, and leaves a remainder; the tenants withhold the owner's fruit and are displaced, turning unpaid produce into a judgment story.

column5: fruit-producing people receive the kingdom
column6: The commentary links fruitful purification with the lasting hereafter; Jesus says the kingdom goes to a people producing its fruits, giving the vineyard's yield an ethical and eschatological measure.

column5: rich farmer stores his abundant harvest for many years
column6: The commentary's field yields product but asks what is lasting; the rich farmer plans to keep his grain for years, setting accumulated crop beside the commentary's question of enduring good.

column5: the farmer dies that night and loses his stored goods
column6: The commentary calls the hereafter better and more lasting than worldly life; the farmer's sudden death interrupts his plan to keep the harvest, making stored produce an unstable remainder.

column5: rich toward oneself versus rich toward God
column6: The commentary ties success to enduring good; Jesus concludes that accumulating goods without being rich toward God misses the lasting measure of success.

column5: fruit leading to sanctification and its end, eternal life
column6: The commentary brings purification and lasting success together; Paul says liberation bears fruit in sanctification and ends in eternal life, giving the ethical fruit an enduring destination.

column5: farmer waits patiently for precious earth's fruit and early and late rain
column6: The commentary presents lasting good as the result of crop growth; James makes a farmer's patience for the precious harvest an example of waiting, adding the time required for yield.

column5: bread cast on waters found after many days
column6: The commentary links a present share with what remains; Ecclesiastes uses casting bread on waters and finding it later, a possible giving-and-return image whose precise sense is debated.

column5: grain that dies bears much fruit
column6: The commentary sets a fading pasture against growth that yields; Jesus' grain image makes loss precede abundant fruit, a specific but differently focused reversal.

column5: body sown perishable and raised imperishable
column6: The commentary opposes perishing pasture to what remains; Paul uses sowing and resurrection to contrast perishable and imperishable bodies, extending the crop's persistence to resurrection.
